directAnswer: Pope Adrian IV was Nicholas Breakspear, the only Englishman to serve as pope, who reigned from 1154 to 1159. A former abbot and papal legate to Scandinavia, he crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor, placed Rome under interdict to expel Arnold of Brescia, and is linked to the disputed bull Laudabiliter concerning Ireland.

sections.h2: Nicholas Breakspear, From Hertfordshire to Saint-Ruf
paras: Nicholas was born around 1100 in Hertfordshire, according to tradition near Abbots Langley. As a young man he went to France and joined the canons regular of Saint-Ruf near Avignon, where he was eventually elected abbot. Complaints from some of his canons brought him to the attention of Eugene III, who made him cardinal bishop of Albano around 1149.

In 1152 Eugene sent him as legate to Scandinavia. He reorganized the Church in Norway, establishing the archdiocese of Nidaros (Trondheim) in 1153 with authority over Norway and the Atlantic islands, and held a council in Sweden that prepared the way for a Swedish archbishopric. His work there earned him lasting respect in the North. On his return he was elected pope on December 4, 1154.

sections.h2: Arnold of Brescia and the Interdict on Rome
paras: The Roman Commune, inspired by Arnold of Brescia, continued to defy papal rule. After a cardinal was attacked in the street, Adrian placed the city of Rome under interdict in 1155, the first time this had happened. With the churches closed during Holy Week, the Romans expelled Arnold. He was later captured and handed over to the city prefect, who had him executed in 1155.

sections.h2: Frederick Barbarossa and the Besançon Incident
paras: Adrian crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor in St. Peter's on June 18, 1155, after a tense dispute at their first meeting over whether the king would perform the ceremonial service of holding the pope's stirrup. Relations soured when Adrian made peace with William I of Sicily in the Treaty of Benevento in 1156.

At the Diet of Besançon in 1157, a papal letter describing the empire as a beneficium conferred by the pope was translated as fief, provoking outrage among the German princes. Adrian later explained he had meant a benefit or good deed, not a feudal grant, but the mistrust endured.

Adrian is associated with Laudabiliter, a bull said to have approved Henry II of England's intervention in Ireland in order to reform its Church. Its text survives only through the writings of Gerald of Wales, and historians still debate whether it is genuine, altered, or a later fabrication. John of Salisbury, a friend of the pope, recorded that Adrian granted Ireland to Henry, though the exact nature of the grant is uncertain.
Adrian died at Anagni on September 1, 1159, and was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Nicholas Breakspear in Hertfordshire around 1100
The only English pope; abbot of the canons regular of Saint-Ruf
As legate, established the archdiocese of Nidaros (Trondheim) in 1153
Crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor on June 18, 1155
Linked to the disputed bull Laudabiliter on Ireland

faqs.question: Was Adrian IV the only English pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nicholas Breakspear of Hertfordshire is the only pope born in England.

faqs.question: Did Adrian IV really give Ireland to Henry II?
faqs.answer: Contemporaries such as John of Salisbury say he made some grant, but the bull Laudabiliter survives only in Gerald of Wales's writings, and historians debate its authenticity and content.

faqs.question: Why did Adrian IV put Rome under interdict?
faqs.answer: In 1155 he used the interdict to pressure the Romans into expelling Arnold of Brescia, whose movement backed the Roman Commune against papal rule.
